items.title: Amazon Timestream for InfluxDB 3 now supports heterogeneous clusters
items.description: Amazon Timestream for InfluxDB 3 now supports heterogeneous clusters, which let you assign a different instance size to each node role in an InfluxDB 3 Enterprise cluster. You can size the writer, reader, and compactor roles independently. You set the size for each role when you create a cluster or add nodes to an existing cluster, using the Amazon Timestream console, the AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), or the AWS SDKs. Time series workloads rarely load every part of a database the same way. Queries need memory for the query cache, writes are gated by durable flushes to object storage, and compaction needs vCPUs to merge files in the background. Because every node previously ran one instance size, scaling a single role meant scaling all of them and paying for headroom on nodes already sized correctly. You can now place reader nodes on a larger size for a bigger cache or more complex queries while keeping writer nodes smaller, or give the compactor more vCPUs without changing the rest of the cluster. There is no additional charge, and you pay the standard price for each node at the size you select. Heterogeneous clusters are available for InfluxDB 3 Enterprise clusters in all AWS Regions where Amazon Timestream for InfluxDB is available. To get started, open the Amazon Timestream console. For more information, see the Amazon Timestream for InfluxDB documentation and pricing page .

items.title: Amazon CloudWatch announces basic OpenTelemetry enrichment at no additional cost
items.description: Amazon CloudWatch now offers basic OpenTelemetry enrichment for AWS service metrics at no additional cost. Basic enrichment turns the metrics that AWS services publish to CloudWatch into OpenTelemetry data points you can query with PromQL. It covers metrics that identify a resource, such as Amazon EC2 CPUUtilization with an InstanceId dimension. Enriched metrics get resource attributes for the Amazon Resource Name, cloud provider, Region, and account ID, plus an instrumentation scope naming the source service. Your original CloudWatch dimensions become data point attributes. To query AWS resource tags as PromQL labels, choose resource tag enrichment instead. It is charged as OTel Vended Metric Enrichment, and you can switch levels at any time. Your AWS service metrics stay available through existing CloudWatch APIs. When you set up CloudWatch Omni, basic enrichment is enabled by default, so you can query your AWS service metrics with PromQL right away. Any account can also enable it directly in the CloudWatch console, AWS Command Line Interface, or the AWS SDKs. Basic enrichment is available in all AWS Regions where CloudWatch OpenTelemetry metrics are supported. To learn more, see AWS vended metrics in OpenTelemetry format . For pricing, see Amazon CloudWatch pricin g.

items.title: Amazon Neptune introduces Neptune Graph Sessions, smaller graphs designed for agents that scale to zero and resume automatically
items.description: Amazon Neptune now supports Neptune Graph Sessions, a compute mode designed for agents that scales memory and CPU automatically and scales to zero when idle. You can give each agent, user or task its own graph without paying for the 16 m-NCU minimum of a provisioned graph. You choose a starting size of 4 s-NCU (sessions Neptune capacity units) or 8 s-NCU of working memory when you create a graph. Applications such as GraphRAG assistants, AI agents and per-user analytics improve accuracy when using a graph. These use cases often need a separate graph for each conversation or task, and the size of that graph is hard to predict. Each Graph Sessions graph starts at the size you choose and includes memory headroom up to twice that size for the data you load and the queries you run (a 4 s-NCU graph has up to 8 s-NCU of memory, and an 8 s-NCU graph has up to 16 s-NCU), so the starting size does not have to cover your largest graph. You are billed for the memory your graph uses, so a graph that fits in the smaller size is billed at the smaller size. When a graph is idle, Graph Sessions scales to zero automatically after 15 minutes, and the graph resumes in seconds when the next query arrives. Your graph and its data are kept, so you do not reload data for each session and pay for the running price. You can create a Neptune Graph Sessions graph using the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs, and query it with openCypher like any other Neptune Analytics graph. For more information, see the Neptune Analytics User Guide and the Amazon Neptune pricing page .

items.title: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL supports minor versions 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20, and 14.25
items.description: Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS) for PostgreSQL now supports the latest minor versions 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20, and 14.25. We recommend that you upgrade to the latest minor versions to address Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) in prior versions of PostgreSQL, and to benefit from the bug fixes and improvements added by the PostgreSQL community. You can upgrade your databases during scheduled maintenance windows using automatic minor version upgrades. To simplify operations at scale, enable automatic minor version upgrades and use the AWS Organizations Upgrade Rollout Policy to orchestrate multiple upgrades in phases, validating on lower-priority environments before upgrading your most critical ones. You can also use Amazon RDS Blue/Green deployments to minimize downtime for minor version upgrades. For more information, see Upgrading RDS for PostgreSQL DB engine . Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL makes it simple to set up, operate, and scale PostgreSQL deployments in the cloud. See Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Pricing for pricing details and regional availability. Create or update a fully managed Amazon RDS database in the Amazon RDS Management Console or by using the AWS Command Line Interface (CLI).

items.title: AWS Lambda now supports orchestrating MicroVMs with Lambda durable functions
items.description: Today, AWS announces a developer preview of a new extension for orchestrating Lambda MicroVMs with Lambda durable functions . The extension adds durable operations for running work on MicroVMs and managing their lifecycle. You can use the new operations to build software factories, security scanners, or orchestrate CI/CD jobs that run untrusted or agent-generated code in isolated sandboxes. With Lambda durable functions, you can build resilient, multi-step applications and AI workflows that run for up to one year, with built-in checkpointing and automatic retries. Lambda MicroVMs are a serverless compute primitive that provides VM-level isolation, near-instant launch and resume, and state preservation for running user-generated or AI-generated code. With this launch, you can run individual tasks in a MicroVM or launch a MicroVM session, where tasks share the same files and memory. The durable function manages the MicroVM lifecycle and runs each task as a durable operation. It checkpoints progress, retries failed tasks, and refreshes MicroVM tokens as needed. A single durable function can orchestrate multiple MicroVMs in parallel, and you can trigger it from event sources such as Amazon SQS or Amazon EventBridge . An optional worker library runs inside your MicroVM image to receive tasks, send heartbeats, and report results. The MicroVM extension is available as a developer preview for the AWS Durable Execution SDK for TypeScript and Python . To get started, add the extensions package to your function alongside the Durable Execution SDK ( JS/TS , Python ) and add the MicroVM worker library ( JS/TS , Python ) to your MicroVM image. Developer preview features may change, so do not use them for production workloads. The extension is available in all AWS Regions that support Lambda durable functions and Lambda MicroVMs. To learn more, see the MicroVM orchestration documentation and the sample application . To share feedback, open an issue in the Durable Execution SDK GitHub repository in JavaScript or Python .

items.title: Amazon CloudWatch Omni now integrates with PagerDuty
items.description: Amazon CloudWatch Omni alerts can now automatically create PagerDuty incidents, so notifications flow directly into your existing incident management workflows. This reduces mean time to resolution (MTTR) by eliminating manual notification steps and ensuring consistent incident workflows.  CloudWatch Omni is a fully managed AI-powered observability experience built on open standards that unifies monitoring for AI agents, applications, and infrastructure. PagerDuty is an incident management platform that routes alerts to the right on-call responders and coordinates their response. When an Omni alert fires, Omni creates a PagerDuty incident. In PagerDuty, Omni alerts follow your existing on-call schedules and escalation policies, so critical alerts reach the right responder wherever they are, at any hour. Omni alerts include severity, the affected service, and a link back to the related data in Omni, so responders have the context they need to diagnose the problem. For PagerDuty integration in Amazon CloudWatch Omni regional availability, see Supported Regions for CloudWatch Omni . To learn more, visit Amazon CloudWatch Omni documentation and refer to the Omni PagerDuty integration page.

items.title: Amazon OpenSearch Service optimised engine now publishes data to Amazon S3 Tables
items.description: The optimized engine for observability in Amazon OpenSearch Service now lets customers who send observability data directly to OpenSearch publish that data to Amazon S3 Tables. These customers can search and analyze data in OpenSearch, but reusing it with other analytics and AI tools often requires a parallel ingestion or custom export pipeline. This integration provides an open-table reuse path without changing how data enters OpenSearch. Publish policies make selected indexes available as Apache Iceberg tables in your AWS account. Engineers and AI agents can query the same observability data with Amazon EMR Serverless, DuckDB, and other Iceberg-compatible tools without adding query load to OpenSearch. They can reuse it for historical investigations, cross-dataset analysis, audits, and long-term trend analysis while retaining it at lower cost. This feature is available at no additional charge on the new engine for observability with OpenSearch 3.9 in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), and Europe (Spain). Amazon S3 Tables storage and the services you use to query the data incur standard charges. To get started, add a publish policy to your optimized domain and see Publish indexes to Amazon S3 Tables in the documentation .

items.title: Elastic Load Balancing for Envoy is now generally available
items.description: Today, AWS announces the general availability of ELB for Envoy, a new load balancer type in Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) that runs open-source Envoy proxies. Platform teams that run Envoy themselves own upgrades, security patching, and capacity across Availability Zones (AZs). ELB for Envoy takes on that work. Each load balancer runs its proxies on dedicated Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instances with hardware isolation from the AWS Nitro System, so a zero-day in Envoy stays contained to your load balancer. ELB for Envoy also monitors for security vulnerabilities (CVEs) and applies Envoy and operating system patches automatically, so you can focus on your applications instead of your proxy fleet. You can bring your existing Envoy configurations, extensions, and control planes as they are, and add AWS integrations such as AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) and AWS WAF with minimal configuration. If you run Envoy Gateway on Kubernetes, install the ELB for Envoy remote infrastructure provider  alongside Envoy Gateway to move your proxies to ELB for Envoy without rewriting your Gateway API resources. You can add custom logic with WebAssembly, Lua scripting, or external processing. ELB for Envoy runs inside your VPC, integrates with Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) security groups, and supports VPC encryption. It's well suited to workloads that need Envoy's extensibility, such as custom authentication, request transformation, or advanced traffic routing, along with Kubernetes ingress and migrations from self-managed Envoy. At general availability, ELB for Envoy is available in 14 AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Ireland), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Stockholm), Europe (Spain), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Hong Kong), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Malaysia), and Asia Pacific (Thailand). To learn more, visit the ELB for Envoy product page , ELB pricing page , and documentation . To get started, visit the AWS Management Console .

items.title: Amazon Transcribe Turbo: more accurate transcripts and natural turn-taking for voice agents, now in public preview
items.description: Amazon Transcribe Turbo, our next-generation speech-to-text model, is now in public preview in US East (Ohio) for batch and streaming. Turbo improves accuracy, supports custom vocabulary, and formats numbers, dates, currency, phone numbers and addresses following each locale's conventions. Streaming: English, Portuguese, French, Italian, German and Spanish supported. Word Error Rate (WER) drops ~14% relative in English and 11% relative in the other languages versus the current production model, and formatting accuracy improves by more than 20 points. Batch: English Turbo is generally available in most AWS Regions. Portuguese, French, Italian, German, Spanish, Chinese, Japanese, Korean and Arabic are now in preview, with ~16% lower word error rate. The base model needs no API, code, or SDK changes. Turbo streaming also adds two new features for voice agents in English at launch and for other languages by the end of December 2026. Semantic turn-taking detects when a caller is done speaking from what they said and their prosody in speech, not silence alone. It won't cut callers off mid-sentence ("I'd like to transfer… $250 to savings") or make short answers like "yes", "no" wait on silence timeouts. It responds in about 615 ms with a 5% interruption rate, and you can tune it. Runtime ASR hints give your agent context at every turn. Unlike static custom vocabulary, set once per session, hints enable your client application to send menu options, expected names and the expected entity type (date, phone number, currency) before each turn. On English customer service data, hints raise menu-routing accuracy from 87% to 97%. Both features come at no additional charge. To try them, turn on EndOfTurnDetection and send hints in a ConfigureEvent. Learn more in the Builder Center blog and the sample voice agent on GitHub .

items.title: AWS IoT Core now uses dedicated IPv6 address ranges for the HTTP rule action
items.description: AWS IoT Core can now send traffic to HTTPS endpoints within a dedicated, published IPv6 address range. This launch enables you to configure your HTTPS endpoints to accept requests only from AWS IoT Core and block all other traffic, thereby reducing your endpoint's exposure to public internet. AWS IoT Core is a fully managed service that securely connects IoT devices at scale to the AWS cloud and routes IoT device data to AWS and third-party services. AWS IoT Core's HTTP rule action delivers IoT device data to any HTTPS endpoint, such as your application servers, on-premises systems, or partner services. With this launch, you can choose from AWS IoT Core's published IPv6 range, and add the fixed IPv6 range to an Amazon API Gateway resource policy , a security group , or your firewall rules . Your HTTPS endpoints will then accept traffic only from AWS IoT Core, giving you network layer control over who can reach your endpoint. To get started, configure your HTTPS endpoint destination to be reachable only over IPv6 by publishing AAAA DNS records (and removing the A DNS records). This allows IoT Core's HTTP rule action to use only IPv6 addresses when sending data to your HTTP destination. Then allow AWS IoT Core's published IPv6 range for your Region, and create or update your HTTP rule action with the endpoint destination. Dedicated IPv6 ranges are available at no additional charge in all AWS Global Regions where AWS IoT Core is available, including AWS GovCloud (US). To find the range for your Region, see Restricting HTTP action traffic to the rules engine IPv6 ranges in the AWS IoT Core Developer Guide.

items.title: AWS IoT Core quotas and usage are now visible in AWS Service Quotas console
items.description: AWS IoT Core now publishes its most used service quotas and your current usage against the quotas in AWS Service Quotas console , improving observability and monitoring of API limits and quotas. This launch enables you to monitor your service quota usage, set alarms before you are throttled, and request quota increases ahead of planned growth. AWS IoT Core is a fully managed service that securely connects IoT devices at scale to the AWS cloud and routes IoT device data to AWS and third-party services. As your device fleet grows, your applications depend on quotas for operations, such as connecting and authenticating devices, publishing and subscribing to messages. Previously, service quotas and usage were not visibile in AWS Service Quotas Console and you had to contact AWS Support to learn about your current utilization before throttling occured. Now you can view quotas and usage for both device messaging (data plane) and resource management (control plane) APIs. You can also use Amazon CloudWatch usage metrics to create alarms that notify you when your usage approaches a quota. To get started, visit AWS Service Quotas console and choose AWS IoT Core. This capability is available at no additional cost. To learn more, see AWS IoT Core quotas in the AWS General Reference and Viewing service quotas in the Service Quotas User Guide.

items.title: AWS Device Farm now supports Android emulators and iOS simulators
items.description: AWS Device Farm , a service for testing mobile and web apps, now supports Android emulators and iOS simulators alongside real devices for automated and manual testing, enabling faster testing at scale early in your development pipeline. With virtual devices, you can shift testing left to stages that need high speed and volume, such as pull requests, code merges, and smoke tests, and keep real devices for later stages that need high fidelity, such as regression and release testing. Virtual devices running the latest supported OS version typically start in seconds, and others start in about a minute. Previously, you could build and maintain your own Android emulator and iOS simulator infrastructure, which requires separate tooling and compute such as Mac hosts for iOS, or run every stage on real devices, which is slower, limited by device availability, and costs more than early-stage testing needs. Now you can use the same fully managed Device Farm APIs, test environment, private endpoint access, and test frameworks for both virtual and real devices. To switch, you change only the device type, so your pipeline and tests stay the same and you avoid maintaining two separate orchestration layers. Virtual devices use the existing metered pricing . For Android, your existing unmetered slots now go further and run either a real or a virtual device at no additional charge. Android emulators and iOS simulators are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Device Farm is offered. To get started, see the AWS Device Farm Developer Guide .

items.title: AWS IAM extends trusted identity propagation to IAM federation and IAM Roles Anywhere, and simplifies it in IAM Identity Center
items.description: Trusted identity propagation (TIP) carries the identity of a human user or workload with requests to supported AWS Services. Customers can use that identity in IAM policy conditions for access control and to identify the originating human user or workload in AWS CloudTrail. AWS is expanding TIP to AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) federation and IAM Roles Anywhere , while simplifying the existing TIP experience in AWS IAM Identity Center. In addition, IAM outbound identity federation now enables customers to request an AWS-signed JSON Web Token (JWT) that includes identity information from TIP sessions, allowing external services to identify the human user or workload that originated the request. With TIP for IAM federation, customers can map the human or workload identity, along with optional runtime claims such as a risk score or a CI/CD workflow name, from the SAML assertion or OIDC token used for federation to the role session. IAM Roles Anywhere extends TIP to identities sourced from X.509 certificates. For IAM Identity Center, which supports workforce identities, the simplified experience adds the username, an identifier provided by your identity source, alongside the user ID that IAM Identity Center generates, and carries this information uniformly whether users access applications or AWS accounts. Across all supported paths, TIP preserves identity information as requests move between IAM roles and AWS services without requiring per-role trust policy updates.  TIP for IAM federation, IAM Roles Anywhere, IAM outbound identity federation, and the simplified IAM Identity Center experience are available in all commercial AWS Regions, the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud (Germany) Region. To get started, see the Trusted Identity Propagation for IAM documentation , Trusted Identity Propagation in IAM Identity Center documentation , and the  TIP launch blog .

Daybreak Red is designed for advanced, authorized tasks such as vulnerability research, exploit reproduction, and mitigation development. For these tasks, a lower refusal threshold, matched by stronger identity verification, monitoring, and access controls, improves the speed and depth of an investigation. Your inference data is not used for model training, and you are not required to opt in to sharing your data with OpenAI. On the bedrock-runtime endpoint, the model is available through the US Gov Geo cross-Region inference (CRIS) profile. Access to the model requires enrollment in Daybreak access from OpenAI. To enroll, contact OpenAI or reach out to your AWS account team for guidance on eligibility. Once approved, work with your account team to request access on AWS. For regional availability through the bedrock-mantle endpoint and more information, view the documentation.

With this launch, customers in the Africa (Cape Town) Region can run agentic AI, search, and observability workloads without provisioning or managing clusters. Compute is fully separated from storage, which lets customers scale compute independently to reduce costs during low-traffic periods while remaining ready for traffic spikes. With scale-to-zero and pay-per-usage pricing, customers can save up to 60% compared to provisioning OpenSearch clusters for peak loads. To learn more, see the OpenSearch Serverless documentation and pricing page . For the full list of AWS Regions where OpenSearch Serverless is available, see the Regional Services List.

items.title: AWS CloudFormation makes resource coverage comprehensive with 206 new types
items.description: AWS CloudFormation now supports 206 additional resource types across 88 services, including Amazon SageMaker Hub, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore PolicyEngine, and Amazon EC2 Snapshot. This closes key gaps in CloudFormation coverage and helps customers to standardize on safe and scalable infrastructure management workflows. The launch utilized a new AI-driven internal framework to collapse the costs of onboarding resource types to CloudFormation, setting up CloudFormation for continued coverage expansion. AWS Cloud Control API supports all new resource types that CloudFormation supports. Additionally, Cloud Control API now supports 224 read-only resource types across 99 services, making it easier to find and inspect existing AWS resources. CloudFormation resource coverage is available across all AWS Regions where the underlying service is available. To learn more, visit the AWS resource and property types reference , the Cloud Control API resource list , and the AWS CloudFormation User Guide .

items.title: Amazon Connect Customer dashboards now support grouping historical metrics by time interval
items.description: Amazon Connect Customer analytics dashboards now support grouping historical metrics by time interval on trailing widgets, giving contact center managers granular control over how performance data is visualized over time. Trailing widgets now display data grouped by 15-minute, 30-minute, one-hour, daily, and weekly intervals. For example, a workforce manager investigating a spike in average handle time can switch from a daily view to 15-minute intervals to pinpoint the exact period the spike occurred, then zoom out to a weekly view to confirm whether it reflects a broader trend. Time interval grouping on dashboards is available in all AWS regions where Amazon Connect Customer is offered. To learn more, see the Amazon Connect Customer Administrator Guide.   To learn more about Amazon Connect Customer, visit the Amazon Connect Customer website .

items.title: Amazon OpenSearch Service optimized engine supports high-cardinality query and DSL
items.description: Amazon OpenSearch Service now supports distributed joins, high-cardinality aggregations, and OpenSearch query DSL on the new engine. Observability data often spans logs, traces, and agent traces. Engineers and their AI agents must connect these datasets to determine what failed, where it failed, and who was affected.     With Piped Processing Language (PPL) or SQL, engineers and agents can query multiple petabytes to connect an error log to its trace and enrich telemetry with service ownership or deployment metadata in one query. High-cardinality aggregations help you measure incident impact across millions of distinct hosts, users, or tenants. Because the new engine distributes joins and aggregations across data nodes, you don’t need to copy related data into a single index. Routing key support keeps related documents on the same shard, so lookups and joins on that key stay fast. The new engine also supports OpenSearch query DSL, so applications, alerts, and integrations that send query DSL get its cost and performance benefits for supported analytics workloads without rewrites. These features are available on OpenSearch 3.9, at no additional charge, in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), and Europe (Spain). To get started, create or upgrade a domain to OpenSearch 3.9 with the new engine. To learn more, see the documentation .

items.title: Amazon RDS for SQL Server now supports up to 500 databases per instance
items.description: Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for SQL Server now supports up to 500 databases per DB instance, up from the previous limit of 100. This higher density helps software as a service (SaaS) providers, multi-tenant applications, and other customers who run many databases on a DB instance. Previously, these customers had to spread their databases across several DB instances. You can use this feature to consolidate databases on fewer DB instances. This simplifies management, reduces the number of DB instances to monitor and patch, and lowers license and infrastructure costs. The 500-database limit applies to DB instances with 4 or more vCPUs (xlarge and larger, excluding burstable instance classes) on all SQL Server versions that Amazon RDS supports. It's available for Single-AZ deployments of Enterprise, Enterprise Developer, Standard, Standard Developer, and Web editions, and for Multi-AZ deployments of Enterprise, Enterprise Developer (using Always On Availability Groups), and Web edition.. Multi-AZ deployments using Database Mirroring, Multi-AZ deployments of Standard Edition, and smaller instances keep their current limits. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for SQL Server is available. To learn more, see Amazon RDS for Microsoft SQL Server User Guide . For pricing details, see Amazon RDS for SQL Server Pricing .

items.title: Amazon EC2 X8i instances are now available in the Asia Pacific (New Zealand) Region
items.description: Starting today, Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) X8i instances are available in the Asia Pacific (New Zealand) Region. These instances are powered by custom Intel Xeon 6 processors available only on AWS. X8i instances are SAP-certified and deliver the highest performance and fastest memory bandwidth among comparable Intel processors in the cloud. They deliver up to 43% higher performance, 1.5x more memory capacity (up to 6TB), and 3.3x more memory bandwidth compared to previous generation X2i instances. X8i instances are designed for memory-intensive workloads like SAP HANA, large databases, data analytics, and Electronic Design Automation (EDA). Compared to X2i instances, X8i instances offer up to 50% higher SAPS performance, up to 47% faster PostgreSQL performance, 88% faster Memcached performance, and 46% faster AI inference performance. X8i instances come in 14 sizes, from large to 96xlarge, including two bare metal options. To get started, visit the AWS Management Console . X8i instances can be purchased via Savings Plans, On-Demand instances, and Spot instances. For more information visit X8i instances page .

items.title: AWS Sign-In introduces configurable Sign-in duration of up to 90 days
items.description: AWS Sign-In now enables developers and AI agents to stay authenticated for up to 90 days without frequent sign-ins or consent prompts. With this launch, administrators can configure Sign-in duration , which controls how long an OAuth Sign-in session remains active, for individual IAM users and roles. This capability reduces authentication interruptions for long-running workflows and provides a more secure alternative to static access keys by using short-lived, renewable credentials. Existing session duration limits remain unchanged unless administrators explicitly configure longer durations. Sign-In Duration supports AWS CLI (aws login), AWS MCP Server, and other OAuth-enabled applications. It does not affect AWS Management Console sessions. Customers can configure the setting using the IAM console, AWS CLI, or IAM API in all AWS commercial Regions. To learn more , see the AWS Sign-In session management User Guide , Configure Sign-In duration on Role User Guid e, Condition Key User Guide

items.title: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports managed observability and user management extensions for Slurm clusters
items.description: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports managed cluster extensions for Slurm clusters. You can install, configure, update, and remove managed features through the SageMaker AI console or API. The first two extensions cover observability and user management. Earlier, every observability or user management change for HyperPod Slurm clusters meant editing lifecycle scripts and then replacing or rerunning nodes. Now, HyperPod manages these features for you, and you keep lifecycle scripts and custom AMIs for your organization's own software. For each extension, you declare a configuration. HyperPod validates it and applies it to every node, including nodes you add later. It then reports the extension's status and the health of each node. The observability extension collects node, GPU, Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA), Slurm job, and Slurm cluster metrics. It sends them to Amazon CloudWatch or Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, and you can add Amazon Managed Grafana dashboards. The user management extension creates users and groups with the same IDs on every node. It also controls who can sign in with SSH and use sudo on each node type, with local users, Active Directory, or both. Cluster extensions are available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker HyperPod is available. You pay only for the AWS resources you use. To learn more, see Cluster extensions in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide, read the launch blog , or visit the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod product page .

items.title: Amazon API Gateway announces API Portal
items.description: Today, Amazon API Gateway announces API Portal , a new feature that discovers, governs, and documents the APIs and AI endpoints behind Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancer, and Amazon CloudFront across your AWS organization. Many organizations can't see which APIs are running, which were never registered, which are no longer maintained, and which lack protection. API Portal builds a continuously updated inventory using AWS-side traffic logs and service configuration records, with nothing to install, no logs to forward, and no traffic to reroute, for a single account or your entire AWS organization. Every discovered API starts as a shadow API until you choose to manage it. API Portal labels each API as public or private and identifies AI endpoints, including MCP servers, A2A servers, and LLM endpoints. For managed APIs, it flags those that stop receiving traffic or lose their owner and evaluates security posture against best practices such as authentication, throttling, and AWS WAF protection. With AWS WAF API Security , it also shows the security events detected per API. You can publish any managed API in a documentation portal for internal teams or external partners, with your branding, Amazon Cognito access control, and interactive Try it pages. If you already use API Gateway Portals, your portals continue to work and are now managed from the Documentation Portals section of API Portal. API Portal is available in 32 AWS Regions; see the Amazon API Gateway FAQ and pricing pages for details. To get started, see the following resources: Amazon API Gateway product page Introducing API and AI security on AWS blog API Portal documentation AWS WAF API Security documentation

items.title: Amazon OpenSearch Service now supports OpenSearch version 3.9
items.description: You can now run OpenSearch version 3.9 on Amazon OpenSearch Service. OpenSearch 3.9 helps you reduce vector memory and storage, evaluate search quality with more large language model (LLM) providers, build more responsive AI agents, and control access to shared resources. This release adds a new half-float vector type and a bf16 encoder, which store each vector dimension in 16 bits to reduce the memory and storage your vector indexes need. New 2-bit and 4-bit scalar quantization lets you choose the right balance of compression and recall for each workload. Base64-encoded vector ingestion makes request payloads smaller, which speeds up bulk loading. In addition, radial search now uses a redesigned graph traversal to improve both recall and throughput. In Search Relevance Workbench, LLM-as-a-Judge now works with Amazon Bedrock and other LLM providers through ML Commons connectors. You can also retry failed documents, edit ratings, and reuse earlier judgments to reduce repeated LLM calls. OpenSearch 3.9 also adds gRPC streaming for model predictions and agent execution. Responses come back token by token, so your agentic applications can show answers as they’re generated. Finally, the new resource sharing and access control framework allows you to share resources such as anomaly detectors and machine learning models with specific users and roles without granting broad access. OpenSearch 3.9 is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon OpenSearch Service is offered. To learn how to upgrade, see Upgrading Amazon OpenSearch Service domains in the Amazon OpenSearch Service Developer Guide.

items.title: AWS WAF introduces simplified pricing
items.description: AWS WAF now offers simplified pricing that follows what you protect instead of how you configure it. Previously, you paid separate charges for each web ACL, rule, rule group subscription, and capacity tier, making every security decision a billing calculation. Now, your bill follows three dimensions: the resources you protect, the traffic AWS WAF inspects, and the level of protection you apply. This makes the cost-benefit trade-off easy to understand, and adding or changing rules no longer changes your rate. This new pricing goes into effect on Feb 1, 2027.  The new model makes protection costs predictable before you deploy. Each web ACL now includes up to 2,500 WCU at no extra charge, up from 1,500, and you can add rules such as Bot Control common protections or the Anti-DDoS rule group without additional fees. You pay a resource fee for each protected resource, a base request fee for every request AWS WAF inspects, and a premium request fee only for traffic evaluated by advanced protections like Bot Control targeted protections, Fraud Control, API Security, and AI Security. AWS WAF's new pricing is effective from Feb 1, 2027 in all AWS commercial Regions, including Cape Town, Hong Kong, Hyderabad, Jakarta, Malaysia, Melbourne, Mumbai, New Zealand, Osaka, Seoul, Singapore, Sydney, Taipei, Thailand, Tokyo, Calgary, Frankfurt, Ireland, London, Milan, Paris, Spain, Stockholm, Zurich, Tel Aviv, Sao Paulo, N. Virginia, Ohio, N. California, Oregon, as well as in AWS GovCloud, China Regions, and AWS Isolated Regions. To learn more, visit the AWS WAF pricing page and review the AWS WAF Developer Guide  as well as the blog post  AWS WAF pricing now follows what you protect, not how you configure it .

items.title: AWS WAF announces automated discovery and protection for LLM, MCP, and A2A endpoints using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
items.description: Automated AI endpoint discovery and protection are now generally available, enabling you to discover language model (LLM), Model Context Protocol (MCP), and Agent2Agent (A2A) endpoints behind Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancers, and Amazon CloudFront across your AWS Organization and protect them using AWS WAF. Discovery is available through the new API Gateway API Portal, which recognizes the AI endpoints among the APIs it discovers automatically from traffic logs and service configuration records, with no agents to deploy or logs to forward. An undocumented, public-facing MCP server appears as a shadow API. For unprotected AI endpoints, customers can enable protection using WAF. Protection is available through the new AWS WAF AI Security managed rule group, which protects your AI endpoints. AWS WAF implements protocol recognition and compliance checks to block malformed MCP and A2A messages. When you enable content inspection, the rule group calls Amazon Bedrock Guardrails InvokeGuardrailsCheck API to detect prompt injection, jailbreak attempts, harmful content in requests, and sensitive information in responses. You can use AI Security alongside other AWS Managed Rules or your own custom rules to protect your applications. Additional fees apply, and Amazon Bedrock charges separately for content inspection calls. Together, API Portal and AI Security provide you a complete solution from discovery of all AI endpoints in your AWS environment to protecting them, without having to write any custom rules. API Portal is available in 32 AWS Regions. See the Amazon API Gateway FAQ for the list. AI Security is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (London), Europe (Stockholm), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Asia Pacific (Sydney). To get started, see the following resources: AWS WAF product page AWS WAF AI Security in the AWS WAF Developer Guide API Portal Developer Guide Introducing API and AI security on AWS, from discovery to protection blog post

items.title: Amazon Connect Customer launches the ability to force logout agents directly from the analytics dashboard
items.description: Amazon Connect Customer now allows supervisors to force logout agents directly from the real-time analytics dashboard, eliminating the need to manually contact agents to end their sessions. Force logout ends all active agent sessions and records the logout event in the Login/Logout report, so agent timecards stay complete. For example, a supervisor identifies an agent who left their workstation without logging out after a shift, and force logs them out from the dashboard, preventing idle time from accruing on the agent's timecard. Agent force logout is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Connect Customer is offered. To learn more about analytics dashboards, see the Amazon Connect Customer Administrator Guide .  To learn more about Amazon Connect Customer, visit the Amazon Connect Customer website .

items.title: Amazon Connect Customer now lets you test AI model version upgrades for automated evaluations
items.description: Amazon Connect Customer now enables managers to test new AI model versions for automated evaluations before switching, so evaluation scores remain consistent through model upgrades. When a new version becomes available, managers can test how it would score the same contacts compared to the current version of the model. This lets managers catch scoring differences across models and adjust evaluation criteria before those differences affect agent performance results. Managers also have the flexibility to choose how evaluation forms handle model updates. They can automatically upgrade to the latest model version for ongoing accuracy improvements or stay on a specific version for consistent scoring. This feature is supported in all AWS commercial regions where Amazon Connect Customer is offered. To learn more, visit our documentation and our webpage .

items.title: Amazon Connect Customer expands automated performance evaluations to 45 new languages
items.description: Amazon Connect Customer now uses generative AI to automate evaluations of human and AI agent performance in 45 additional languages, such as Arabic, Dutch, Indonesian, and Polish. Managers define custom evaluation criteria in natural language and receive AI-generated evaluations with justifications in their preferred language. Performance evaluations also support cross-language evaluation and can complete assessments in English, even when the conversation is in another language. This enables multilingual contact centers to use a standardized evaluation framework across languages. This feature is supported in all AWS commercial regions where Amazon Connect Customer is offered. For information about Amazon Connect pricing, please visit our pricing page . To learn more, visit our documentation and our webpage .

items.title: Amazon CloudFront is now available in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud
items.description: Amazon CloudFront is now available in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud. Organizations with strict EU sovereignty requirements can now deliver websites, applications, and APIs with the performance, security, and scale of CloudFront, all within the EU. Until now, customers had to build and run their own delivery and TLS termination infrastructure to keep traffic and data inside the EU. With CloudFront in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, content delivery, TLS termination, logs, and customer configuration stay within the European Sovereign Cloud boundary. The AWS European Sovereign Cloud is physically and logically separate from other AWS Regions, and only EU-resident personnel operate it. This helps governments, healthcare, financial services and other regulated industries meet data residency and operational sovereignty requirements without trading away performance and scale. Customers use the same CloudFront APIs and console experience they already know making it easy to transfer over existing deployments and automations. If you plan to run media streaming or other high-volume workloads, contact your AWS account team and we can help you find the right solution, including options in AWS commercial Regions. To get started, sign in to your AWS European Sovereign Cloud account and create a distribution in the CloudFront console. To learn more about available features and pricing, see the CloudFront Developer Guide  and CloudFront pricing page in ESC .

items.title: AWS Partner Central expands analytics access with Partner Central Agents and Data Subscriptions
items.description: AWS Partners and AWS Marketplace sellers now have two new ways to access their analytics data in AWS Partner Central. Partner Central Agents answer questions in plain language, and Data Subscriptions deliver Partner Central data to an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket every day. Partner Central Agents answer questions about leads, marketing campaigns, opportunities and pipeline, and funding, without navigating dashboards or exporting to spreadsheets. AWS Marketplace sellers can also ask about usage, agreements and renewals, billing, collections, and disbursements. Partners can get the same answers in their own artificial intelligence (AI) assistants and agents through the Partner Central Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. Data Subscriptions deliver ready-to-use datasets to an S3 bucket daily, covering leads, marketing campaigns, partner account relationships, opportunities and pipeline, and AWS Marketplace usage, agreements, and renewals. Because the data lives in a partner's own S3 bucket, partners can connect it to the tools of their choice, such as a business intelligence (BI) tool, a customer relationship management (CRM) system like Salesforce or HubSpot, or a generative AI assistant, and build the reports they need. Both features use existing AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and permissions, so partners see only the data they are already allowed to see, and exported data stays in their own AWS account. These capabilities are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Partner Central is available. To get started, sign in to AWS Partner Central and ask an analytics question, such as "What are my top opportunities this quarter?" To set up Data Subscriptions, choose Settings , and then choose Data Subscriptions . To learn more, see Data Subscriptions in the Partner Central Guide .

items.title: AgentCore runtime instances are now generally available in the AWS GovCloud (US-West) Region
items.description: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime instances are now available in the AWS GovCloud (US-West) Region. Runtime instances run your agents on Amazon EC2 instances in your own account, while AgentCore handles provisioning, patching, scaling, and lifecycle management. With runtime instances, teams in AWS GovCloud (US) can choose GPU-accelerated, memory-optimized, or compute-optimized instance types for their agents and run agent sessions of up to 14 days. Agent instances, storage volumes, and session data stay in the AWS GovCloud (US-West) Region, which helps public sector organizations and their partners meet data residency and compliance requirements. Runtime instances work alongside the default serverless, microVM-based AgentCore runtime, so you can pick the right compute for each agent without changing how you deploy or invoke it. You are charged for the management of the compute provisioned, in addition to your Amazon EC2 costs. To get started, visit AWS News Blog or AgentCore documentation . To learn about pricing, visit AgentCore pricing .

items.title: Amazon CloudFront Announces HTTP/2 Support for Connections to Origins
items.description: Amazon CloudFront now supports HTTP/2 connections to custom origins and VPC origins. HTTP/2 lets CloudFront send many requests over fewer connections to your origin. This means fewer connections and TLS handshakes for your origin to handle, which improves performance for API and agentic workloads, such as AI agents calling MCP servers or mobile and web apps calling backend APIs. Until now, CloudFront connected to origins only over HTTP/1.1, which handles one request at a time per connection. When traffic spiked, for example when an AI agent made many tool calls at once, CloudFront had to open more origin connections. Each new connection added latency and load. With HTTP/2, those requests share connections, so your origin does less work and responds faster. HTTP/2 is also supported for WebSocket connections that support extended CONNECT. If your origin doesn't support HTTP/2, CloudFront automatically falls back to HTTP/1.1, so you don't need to change anything on your origin. HTTP/2 to origins is available from all CloudFront edge locations. There is no additional cost for using HTTP/2 to origins. To learn more, visit Origin HTTP version in the CloudFront Developer Guide.

items.title: AWS Quick adds identity-aware access via 3LO for Snowflake and Databricks structured data sources
items.description: AWS Quick now supports three-legged OAuth (3LO) with end-user permissions for Snowflake and Databricks. When end users in AWS Quick consume Chat, interactive dashboards, or Apps, queries run using their own Snowflake or Databricks identity. Governance policies configured in Snowflake or Databricks Unity Catalog, including applicable row- and column-level controls and access to tables and views, are enforced by the source platform without requiring teams to recreate those policies in Quick. To get started, an administrator adds an OAuth client application in Quick account settings. Data curators then create a Snowflake or Databricks data source, choose 3LO, and turn on trusted identity propagation so each user's identity is passed to the source. End-user permissions through 3LO are supported only for DirectQuery datasets. This feature is available in Quick regions here . To learn more, see Using Snowflake with AWS Quick and Setting up identity enforcement with Databricks 3LO .

items.title: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now detects and recovers hung training jobs on Slurm clusters
items.description: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports hung job detection for Slurm-orchestrated clusters, which finds training jobs that have stopped making progress and returns them to the job queue. SageMaker HyperPod helps you provision resilient clusters for training and deploying AI/ML models. Previously, a job that hung on an NCCL timeout, a stalled data pipeline, or a deadlock kept its GPUs while Slurm reported it as running, until you noticed that the job is not making progress. Now, if a training run hangs, HyperPod detects it within minutes from the job's output and GPU activity, or from log patterns that you define, such as your training step message or an NCCL error, and writes an event to Amazon CloudWatch. You can also have HyperPod cancel the hung job and let Slurm requeue it, so the job can restart from its last checkpoint instead of holding its GPUs idle. You turn on detection per job with an environment variable that points to a rules file, and it works with any framework, including PyTorch, TensorFlow, and JAX, without changes to your code or containers. Hung job detection is available for HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Slurm in all AWS Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available.To learn more, see hung job detection in the user guide and the blog post .

items.title: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod extends AMI auto-patching to Slurm and inference on EKS
items.description: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now automatically patches AMIs on Slurm clusters and introduces a new AMI patching strategy for Amazon EKS clusters that deploy inference workloads. SageMaker HyperPod is purpose-built infrastructure for training and deploying foundation models at scale. Previously, patching a Slurm cluster meant waiting for training runs to finish, scheduling downtime, and upgrading nodes by hand, which could take days of coordination between infrastructure admins and research scientists. Also, auto-patching on Amazon EKS waited for nodes to go idle, which suited training workloads but left nodes serving inference workloads, which rarely go idle, without critical AMI updates. Now, HyperPod patches both while jobs and models keep running: Auto-patching (Slurm): HyperPod patches each node only when it is idle, so running jobs aren't disrupted. Teams no longer have to choose between training and security, and can keep clusters secure without coordination between infrastructure admins and research scientists. Each HyperPod AMI has an ImageReleaseVersion that follows semantic versioning (major.minor.patch) across the NVIDIA driver, CUDA, EFA, NCCL, and OS kernel. Auto-patching applies only patch-level updates to the version you select (for example, 1.4.x), so you get security fixes without upgrades that could break your training jobs. DrainFirst patching strategy (Amazon EKS): HyperPod patches nodes that run inference workloads in rolling batches, draining pods while respecting your Pod Disruption Budgets, so your model keeps serving. If a drain times out, you choose whether HyperPod force-evicts the remaining pods for an urgent patch or skips the node to protect a critical model deployment. When a patch AMI is released, HyperPod schedules the patch 21 days out and notifies you through AWS Health. You can apply it earlier, defer it up to 60 days measured from the patch AMI release date, or turn it off. These capabilities are available in all AWS Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available. To learn more, see Amazon SageMaker HyperPod AMI automatic patching in the user guide.

items.title: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now detects Kubernetes issues affecting training
items.description: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now detects Kubernetes issues that disrupt training, such as crash-looping device plugins or missing DaemonSets, on clusters orchestrated by Amazon EKS. SageMaker HyperPod is purpose-built infrastructure for AI/ML model development, with built-in fault tolerance and automated cluster recovery. Previously, when a device plugin crash-looped or a taint evicted a job's pods, the job's error rarely named the pod or node, so engineers pieced the cause together from kubectl output and per-rank logs. Now, the new HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent watches nodes, critical pods such as NVIDIA device plugins, and required DaemonSets that impact HyperPod and Kubeflow training jobs. The agent correlates Kubernetes issues with the training jobs they affect and reports them as Kubernetes events and Amazon CloudWatch logs. For example, if a device plugin keeps crashing on one node mid training run, the agent flags the node as it loses GPUs and, when the job fails, logs the failure reason with the pods and nodes involved, so you can fix that node and restart sooner. For jobs that opt in, it also shows which rank fell behind when NCCL communication stalls, while the job is still running. The agent is available for HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon EKS in all AWS Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available and you can install it with a helm chart. To learn more, see Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent in the user guide and the blog post .

items.title: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod deep health check now validates training correctness
items.description: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon EKS now support MultiNodeTrainingValidation, a deep health check that validates nodes train correctly before your jobs run. SageMaker HyperPod is purpose-built infrastructure for AI/ML model development, with built-in fault tolerance and automated cluster recovery. Previously, a GPU with a subtle fault could pass hardware stress and connectivity tests and still compute wrong results, and the first sign was often NaN or infinite loss in a production training run. Now, The new MultiNodeTraining Validation check trains a fixed Megatron-LM workload on each instance and then across instances over Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA), and fails any instance whose training loss is NaN, infinite, or diverging, or whose training doesn't finish in time. For example, you can run the check before a multi-week pre-training run, and with automatic node recovery, HyperPod reboots or replaces any instance that fails, so a faulty GPU doesn't surface days later with numerical faults in your training. You can also configure HyperPod to run the check whenever it adds instances, so new and replaced instances are validated before any jobs are scheduled on them. MultiNodeTrainingValidation deep health check is available for HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon EKS in all AWS Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available. To learn more about MultiNodeTrainingValidation, see deep health checks in the user guide and the blog post .

items.title: RDS PostgreSQL now supports PostgreSQL 19.0 in the Amazon RDS Database Preview Environment
items.description: Starting today, Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL 19.0 is available in the Amazon RDS Database Preview Environment , allowing you to evaluate PostgreSQL 19.0 on Amazon RDS PostgreSQL. PostgreSQL 19.0 introduces the REPACK command with a CONCURRENTLY option, which removes table and index bloat with minimal locking. You can now enable parallel autovacuum for faster index vacuuming, and logical replication to synchronize sequence values to the subscriber. Two new extensions, pg_plan_advice and pg_stash_advice, let you guide query planner decisions. Refer to the PostgreSQL community announcement for more details. Amazon RDS Database Preview Environment DB clusters are retained for a maximum period of 60 days and are automatically deleted after the retention period, along with their backups and snapshots. A snapshot created in the Preview Environment cannot be copied to a production environment. You can use the PostgreSQL dump and load functionality to import or export your databases from the Preview Environment. Amazon RDS Database Preview Environment DB clusters are priced as per the pricing in the US East (Ohio) Region.

items.title: AWS Quick brings AI-ready capabilities to your existing datasets
items.description: Today, AWS Quick makes your legacy datasets AI ready through the new technology stack used by its improved visual data preparation experience. This stack powers Dataset Semantics, topics and semantic models, and Dataset Evaluation. Data curators can add business context through dataset descriptions, column descriptions, and custom instructions. They can then compare answer accuracy before and after semantic enrichment to assess how well AI answers reflect their business definitions. When authors edit a supported legacy dataset, AWS Quick automatically opens it in the visual data preparation experience, carrying over its existing data sources, joins, transformations, and calculated fields. Authors can then add semantics and evaluate answer accuracy without recreating the dataset. The visual data preparation experience runs on a new technology stack for structured data, introduced in October 2025. It supports visual, multi-step transformations such as Append, Aggregate, and Pivot, faster ingestion for larger datasets, and up to 20 times higher cross-source join limits than the legacy experience. To make this architecture available to more legacy datasets, AWS Quick has expanded support for Google Sheets and Salesforce connectors, JODA date formats, incremental refresh, and preservation of existing unmaterialized calculated columns during legacy dataset upgrades. This capability is available in all supported AWS Quick Regions . To learn more, see the documentation .

items.title: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports NCCL profiling for training jobs
items.description: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) profiling with the HyperPod NCCL Profiler, giving you visibility into communication performance across the nodes and GPUs in a distributed training job. SageMaker HyperPod helps you scale generative AI model development across hundreds or thousands of AI accelerators. Previously, one throttled GPU or degraded link could slow the whole job without an error, and finding it meant stopping the job to run NCCL tests. Now, the HyperPod NCCL profiler loads as a plugin in your training job and sends per-rank bandwidth and timing to Amazon CloudWatch or Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, with no changes to your training code. For example, if training throughput drops with no errors, the NCCL profiler dashboard on Amazon Managed Grafana flags the node whose GPUs fall behind their peers and shows whether they are throttled, so you find it without stopping the job. If cross-node bandwidth drops on every node at once, the dashboard shows that too, so you can tell a network problem from a faulty GPU. This profiler is available for clusters orchestrated by Amazon EKS or Slurm in all AWS Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available. To learn more, see Observability for clusters orchestrated with Amazon EKS and Observability extension configuration for Slurm in the user guide.

items.title: AWS Global Accelerator now preserves client IPs for NLBs with TLS listeners
items.description: AWS Global Accelerator now preserves the client IP address for traffic sent to Network Load Balancer (NLB) endpoints with TLS listeners. You can terminate TLS at your NLB and still see the original client IP address in your application. This means you can apply security groups, geo-blocking, rate limiting, fraud detection, audit logging, allowlists, and compliance controls based on the real client IP. Previously, you couldn't add an NLB with a TLS listener to an accelerator that had client IP address preservation enabled. You had to choose between terminating TLS at the NLB and seeing the real client IP address. With this launch, you get both. This helps with workloads that need TLS termination at Layer 4, such as non-HTTP TCP protocols, applications that require static or Elastic IP addresses, and high-throughput traffic where a Layer 7 load balancer isn't a fit. To enable this feature, add an NLB with a TLS listener as an endpoint to an accelerator with client IP address preservation setting turned on, the same way you add any NLB. No additional configuration is required! Client IP address preservation for NLBs with TLS listeners is available at no additional charge in all AWS commercial Regions, excluding the AWS GovCloud (US) and China Regions. Standard Global Accelerator pricing applies. To learn more, see Client IP address preservation in the AWS Global Accelerator Developer Guide and Create a listener for your Network Load Balancer in the User Guide for Network Load Balancers.

items.title: Announcing metal size for Amazon EC2 G7 instances
items.description: Today, AWS announces the general availability of the metal size for Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) G7 instances, accelerated by NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs. G7 instances deliver up to 4.6x AI inference performance and up to 2.1x graphics performance compared to G6. Customers can use the metal size of G7 instances to run physical AI simulations, deploy AI agent sandboxes, and accelerate graphics workloads that need direct access to bare metal infrastructure. G7 metal instances enable customers to run specialized workloads that require a custom virtualization stack, hypervisor-level GPU drivers, or licensing-restricted applications. The metal size of G7 instances feature 8 NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs with 32 GB of memory per GPU and custom Intel Xeon 6 processors. They support 192 virtual CPUs (vCPUs), 768 GiB of system memory, and 700 Gbps of Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking bandwidth. The new metal size is available in the AWS US East (N. Virginia) Region. You can purchase G7 metal instances as On-Demand Instances, Spot Instances, or as part of Savings Plans. To get started, use the AWS Management Console , AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), or AWS SDKs. To learn more, visit the G7 instance page .

items.title: Amazon Aurora serverless for MySQL now supports up to 384 ACUs
items.description: Amazon Aurora serverless now supports database capacity of up to 384 Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs) for Aurora MySQL-Compatible Edition, a 50% increase from the previous maximum of 256 ACUs. Each ACU provides approximately 2 gibibytes (GiB) of memory with corresponding CPU and networking, so a single Aurora serverless database can now scale up to 768 GiB of memory. When the workload completes, Aurora serverless automatically scales down to zero. This makes Aurora serverless especially well-suited for agentic AI applications, which typically have bursts of activity, long idle windows, and unpredictable traffic patterns. Aurora serverless handles all of it automatically, scaling capacity with your agents, so you only pay for what you use.    With 384 ACU support, customers can now use Aurora serverless for even more demanding workloads while continuing to scale down to zero when not in use, paying only for the capacity consumed. For new clusters, select a supported Aurora MySQL engine version and set your maximum capacity up to 384 ACUs. For existing clusters on Platform Version 4, simply modify the cluster to update the maximum capacity setting (and the engine version if needed). There will be no downtime if your database is already on Platform Version 4. For existing clusters on older platform versions, upgrade to Platform Version 4 through a pending maintenance action. 384 ACU support is available for Aurora MySQL versions 3.14 and 8.4.10, running on Platform Version 4.    To learn more, see Aurora serverless capacity in the Amazon Aurora User Guide. For pricing details and Region availability, visit Amazon Aurora Pricing . To get started, create or modify an Aurora serverless database in the AWS Management Console .

items.title: Amazon SageMaker Studio now supports training job submission and model deployment for SageMaker HyperPod clusters
items.description: Amazon SageMaker Studio now provides a native developer experience for Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, enabling data scientists to submit distributed training jobs, deploy models, and monitor workloads through a visual interface on HyperPod clusters orchestrated with Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). SageMaker HyperPod is a purpose-built infrastructure for distributed training and fine-tuning of foundation models at scale, designed to reduce infrastructure management overhead. Submitting training jobs and deploying custom models on HyperPod at scale requires familiarity with kubectl and authoring Kubernetes manifests, creating operational burden for data scientists who prefer to work in an interactive development environment. With this launch, data scientists can now submit distributed PyTorch and Ray training jobs and deploy models from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, Amazon S3, or Amazon FSx, through single-page forms with a live YAML preview in SageMaker Studio. Compute configurations in the forms provide reusable resource presets that data scientists select when submitting training jobs or deploying models, eliminating manual compute entry. Metrics and logs are embedded directly in the detail pages, powered by HyperPod Observability and Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, surfacing Kubernetes conditions and events, CloudWatch logs, and embedded metrics so data scientists can diagnose workloads without leaving their environment. For teams managing multiple workloads and using HyperPod task governance, Studio provides a unified queue view where users can see all pending tasks across training jobs and inference services, and adjust a task's priority class directly to optimize cluster utilization. These updates are available for HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon EKS, in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker HyperPod and Amazon SageMaker Studio are currently supported. To learn more, visit the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod in Studio documentation .

items.title: Amazon Connect Customer AI agents now fill in step-by-step guides
items.description: AI agents in Amazon Connect Customer can now populate fields of a step-by-step guide for contact center agents during live customer interactions. With step-by-step guides, managers can design forms and other user interfaces for common workflows, such as rebooking a trip or submitting a claim. Now, AI agents can fill in a guide when it first loads and suggest updates during live conversations, saving time and improving data accuracy. When contact center agents speak to customers, they spend valuable time recording the information they need to solve the customer's problem in a step-by-step guide. For example, when a traveler calls an airline to change her flight, the agent might record her booking reference, dates of travel, and seat preferences. Now, Connect Customer's AI agents can automatically suggest and populate information like this, based on the context of the conversation. Human agents can review each suggestion, accept or reject suggestions individually or in bulk, and make any edits before submitting. The agent can focus on the customer and the problem at hand rather than on manual data entry. You can use AI agents with step-by-step guides in the following AWS regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London). To learn more and get started, see step-by-step guides in the Amazon Connect Customer administrator guide.

items.title: Amazon Inspector expands runtime reachability analysis for ECR and EC2 findings
items.description: Amazon Inspector has expanded its vulnerability management capabilities with runtime reachability analysis for findings originating from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) and Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instances. Previously, Inspector reported every vulnerability found in a resource, including packages that were never used by applications. Security teams had to manually assess which vulnerabilities actually posed risk in their deployed environments. Now, Inspector automatically identifies which vulnerabilities are potentially reachable by analyzing package placement in container images and process activity on EC2 instances. With runtime reachability analysis, you can focus remediation efforts on vulnerabilities that matter most to your security posture. For container images, Inspector determines whether a vulnerable package is within your application's dockerfile paths defined by WORKDIR, ENTRYPOINT, or CMD instructions. For EC2 instances, Inspector identifies whether a vulnerable package was observed running as a process during the most recent scan. For EC2, customers must use the Inspector VM Scanner for agent-based scanning to get this capability. This helps organizations managing large container fleets or complex applications prioritize remediation by distinguishing between vulnerabilities that are potentially reachable versus those in unused dependencies, reducing noise and enabling development and security teams to work more efficiently. Newly generated findings will have runtime reachability analysis included, and backfill of existing findings will be completed over time. Runtime reachability for Inspector findings is available at no additional charge and is available in all AWS Regions where Inspector is already available. To learn more, visit the Amazon Inspector product page .

items.title: AWS CodeDeploy now supports suspending Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling processes
items.description: AWS CodeDeploy can now suspend Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling processes during EC2 in-place deployments to Auto Scaling groups. CodeDeploy is a fully managed service that automates application deployments to Amazon EC2 instances, on-premises servers, AWS Lambda functions, and Amazon ECS services. This launch helps prevent scaling activities from terminating or replacing instances while CodeDeploy is updating them, which can cause a deployment to fail. You can choose to suspend any combination of these processes (Terminate, AZRebalance, InstanceRefresh, and ScheduledActions) on a deployment group, or on a single deployment. CodeDeploy suspends the processes you choose before it deploys and resumes them when the deployment succeeds, fails, or is stopped, so you don't need custom scripts to suspend and resume processes during deployments. A setting on the deployment group applies to every deployment in that group, including deployments that your existing pipelines start. You can configure this feature by using the CodeDeploy console, AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), or AWS SDKs. This feature is available in all AWS Regions , including the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China Regions. To learn more, see Suspending Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling processes during deployments in the AWS CodeDeploy User Guide , or visit the AWS CodeDeploy product page .

items.title: AWS WAF announces automated discovery and protection for API endpoints
items.description: Automated API discovery and protection are now generally available, enabling you to discover every API behind Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancers, and Amazon CloudFront across your AWS Organization and protect them using AWS WAF. Discovery is available through the new API Gateway API Portal, which identifies the APIs automatically from traffic logs and service configuration records, with no agents to deploy or logs to forward. The API Portal classifies the APIs it finds, identifies zombie and shadow APIs, evaluates each API's security posture, and reports findings, including the ones that are missing WAF protections. For unprotected APIs, customers can enable protection using WAF. Protection is available through the new AWS WAF API Security managed rule group, which protects your APIs against the most exploited API attack categories: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA), where the attackers change record IDs in requests to read other users' data, Broken Authentication and Credential Stuffing, where the attackers forge tokens or try stolen passwords at scale, and API Reconnaissance and Enumeration, where the attackers map an API by guessing hidden routes and probing for exposed docs. The events detected by WAF are consolidated into the API Portal findings to provide a complete security picture of your APIs. You can use API Security alongside other AWS Managed Rules or your own custom rules to protect your applications. Together, API Portal and API Security provide you a complete solution from discovery of all APIs in your AWS environment to protecting them, without having to write any custom rules. API Portal is available in 32 AWS Regions. See the Amazon API Gateway FAQ for the list. API Security is available in all AWS Regions where AWS WAF is available, except the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, the China Regions, and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud. To get started, see the following resources: AWS WAF product page AWS WAF API Security in the AWS WAF Developer Guide API Portal Developer Guide Introducing API and AI security on AWS, from discovery to protection blog post

items.title: AWS Device Farm launches Device Connect for local access to remote Android devices
items.description: AWS Device Farm , a service for testing mobile and web apps, now offers Device Connect. With Device Connect, you and AI agents can use remote Android devices from your local machine in an IDE, terminal, or development environment of your choice, as if it were plugged into your laptop. You can attach a debugger, profile performance, preview builds, run ADB (Android Debug Bridge) commands, and interact manually with the devices. You also get live video along with device and test logs. Tools and test frameworks that work with ADB locally now run on a real device that Device Farm manages for you. Previously, you used Device Farm devices manually in a web browser or for automated tests through APIs. You couldn't reach them from your local tools, such as Android Studio or a terminal. Device Connect closes that gap by connecting your local machine to a device hosted in AWS. Your existing ADB-based workflows run unchanged. To get started, install the Device Connect client from GitHub, create a remote access session on Device Farm, and attach to the session's device with the 'devicefarm-connect' command. Device Connect supports Android OS versions nine and later. The client runs on macOS, Linux, and Windows with no additional cost. Device usage is billed at standard Device Farm rates. Device Connect is available in the US West (Oregon) AWS Region. To learn more, see the AWS Device Farm Developer Guide .

items.title: Amazon SageMaker AI now supports viewing capacity reservations
items.description: Amazon SageMaker AI now lets you view SageMaker Capacity Reservations in the SageMaker console, AWS CLI, and AWS SDKs. Previously, customers had no self-service way to see their reserved capacity, including reservation timelines and instance availability, and had to rely on AWS Support to plan their own workloads. Starting today, administrators can review the capacity they hold without leaving SageMaker AI. Administrators can list reservations with their status, instance type, availability zone, instance count, start time, and end time. Customers can view their SageMaker Capacity Reservations under Reserved Capacity section in SageMaker Console. They can open a reservation to see its details, including the ML reservation ARN to use in a SageMaker Inference Endpoint configuration. Additionally, the details page lists the SageMaker AI resources that can use the reservation, such as Amazon SageMaker HyperPod clusters and SageMaker Inference endpoints, and shows the status of each association. This capability is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker HyperPod is available. To learn more, see Amazon SageMaker HyperPod available regions and the Amazon SageMaker AI user guide .

items.title: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod launches a redesigned console experience for creating Amazon EKS-orchestrated clusters
items.description: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now offers a redesigned AWS Management Console experience for creating clusters orchestrated by Amazon EKS. A guided workflow helps ML infrastructure administrators and platform teams set up networking, instance groups, storage, permissions, resiliency, observability, lifecycle scripts, and tags. Required settings are kept apart from optional ones. You enter only what is needed to create the cluster and add other capabilities later, when you need them. You can start with smart defaults or choose a workload profile that applies a coordinated set of settings based on how you plan to use the cluster. You can then adjust individual and advanced settings as needed, reducing repetitive setup while retaining control over the configuration. The redesigned experience is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker HyperPod is available. To learn more, check our documentation .

items.title: AWS DevOps Agent adds Access Profiles and AWS Organizations
items.description: AWS DevOps Agent now gives you more ways to govern and control your AWS DevOps Agent instances.
